title: KV cache retention regulator and atomic invalidation protocol
creator: Sofia Patel
description:
Problem:
Our current KV caching behavior mixes LRU and simple TTL heuristics and relies on eviction passes that run asynchronously from batching boundaries. This causes two practical correctness issues: (1) rare but observable stale KV reads when model rollouts and prefix pinning overlap with eviction, and (2) unpredictable OOMs under bursty continuous-batching patterns because memory accounting happens per-eviction-pass rather than per-request window.

Goal:
Design and implement a "Retention Regulator" and an "Atomic Invalidation Protocol" that enforce strong correctness invariants for prefix-aware KV caching while improving GPU memory predictability for continuous batching workloads. The design should: (a) make eviction decisions deterministic with respect to batch boundaries, (b) preserve model-version and prefix consistency guarantees (no stale KV references after a model or prefix unpin), and (c) provide fine-grained soft/hard retention controls (TTL + generational LRU) to hit target memory budgets without harming latency SLOs.

High-level approach:
- Introduce an in-memory retention regulator component co-located with the KV shard manager that maintains per-tenant/per-model retention state: soft_ttl, hard_ttl, and generation_id.
- Eviction policy combines three axes: prefix-aware reservation, generation-aware LRU (generational garbage collection), and adaptive hard-TTL enforced at batch commit time. Soft TTLs allow opportunistic eviction; hard TTLs are enforced deterministically at the next batch boundary.
- Atomic invalidation tokens: when control-plane actions (model rollout, prefix unpin, or quantization switch) change retention state, we emit an invalidation token (monotonic sequence) attached to subsequent requests. Eviction and KV reads compare tokens to ensure that any entry created under an older token is either used only if pinned by the active request token or rejected. This enables lock-free, wait-free invalidations that still guarantee no stale pointers remain in active batches.
- GPU memory accounting moves from coarse periodic scans to an amortized per-batch credit system. Each batch gets a memory credit budget; cache admits or rejects prefix pinning based on available credits and worst-case token growth for the batch.
- Shadow-eviction pass: a lightweight dry-run eviction executed ahead of the hard-TTL enforcement window to predict memory pressure and optionally throttle incoming batch admission for short intervals instead of triggering full evictions mid-batch.

Correctness invariants (must be proven and tested):
1) No-stale-read: If a request R observes KV entry E, then E was written under an invalidation token T_w and R's token T_r >= T_w or E is pinned explicitly for R's token.
2) Atomic-unpin: Unpin operations (prefix unpin, model decommission) appear atomic at batch boundaries — either all active requests observe the pin or none do.
3) Memory-safety: The regulator ensures worst-case resident GPU memory <= configured budget + small bounded slack (by design slack), preventing OOMs during continuous-batching bursts.

Implementation plan:
- Phase 1 (design + spec): formalize token semantics, batch commit hooks, and regulator API. Draft design doc and state transition diagrams.
- Phase 2 (prototype): implement token plumbing and deterministic hard-TTL enforcement tied to batch commit; add per-batch memory credits and a CLI toggle.
- Phase 3 (safety nets): implement shadow-eviction and admission throttling; add metrics and abort paths for graceful degradation.
- Phase 4 (tests + rollout): add unit tests, property-based tests for invariants, integration benchmarks and canary rollout on a dedicated cluster using runtime-2.3.1.

Testing & metrics:
- Property tests that fuzz concurrent model rollouts + unpins + read/write patterns to validate No-stale-read and Atomic-unpin invariants.
- Benchmarks: eviction latency distribution, batch tail-latency, and OOM incidence rate under synthetic bursty traffic.
- Dashboards: per-tenant resident memory, generation churn rate, invalidation token lag, admission throttle events.

Rollout plan:
- Nightly feature flag behind runtime.eviction.regulator; default disabled.
- Canary on dedicated capacity cluster with synthetic workload; monitor metrics for 48h.
- Gradual ramp to 10% then 50% traffic with automatic rollback on SLO regressions or memory spikes.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Slight increase in request path bookkeeping (token attach) may add small p50 p99 overhead; we aim to mitigate by piggybacking token on existing batch metadata and aggressive in-memory caches for token comparisons.
- Conservative hard-TTL enforcement may temporarily increase eviction churn; shadow-eviction and admission throttling aim to reduce unnecessary churn.

Success criteria:
- Zero production incidents of stale-KV reads during rollout (monitored via synthetic invariants probes).
- Resident GPU memory variance reduced by >= 40% under bursty continuous-batching compared to baseline.
- No more than 2% increase in p99 token attach overhead.
